READING

**Laying out the Vantwyn arithmetic**

Pollination revenue: 400 colonies × £168 = £67,200 a season.

Against that, three deductions:

| Item | Working | Season cost |
|---|---|---|
| Lost Kirkhallow borage | 400 × £71 | £28,400 |
| Spray replacement colonies | 400 × 9% = 36 colonies × £210 | £7,560 |
| Haulage and labour | given | £6,900 |
| **Total deductions** | | **£42,860** |

Net annual operating surplus from the Vantwyn engagement: £67,200 − £42,860 = **£24,340 a season**.

Over three seasons that is **£73,020 in cumulative operating advantage** that Trevannock earns over Ormscleuch.

Those 400 colonies come back in time for heather, so only the borage (£71/colony) is a lost crop, not the full home return of roughly £223 per colony. I have treated only the borage as the opportunity cost, which is the most generous reading of Trevannock.

---

**The equipment comparison**

Ravensgate offer today: £96,000 — firm, closing 2026-11-28.
Lorry residual after the vale permit lapses 2030-01-01: ~£20,000.

Nominal equipment premium sacrificed under Trevannock: £96,000 − £20,000 = **£76,000**.

That £76,000 is received now. The £73,020 operating advantage under Trevannock is earned in instalments across 2027, 2028 and 2029. At even a modest 5 % cost of capital, the present value of the three annual tranches is roughly:

- 2027 (1 year): £24,340 / 1.05 = £23,181  
- 2028 (2 years): £24,340 / 1.105 = £22,031  
- 2029 (3 years): £24,340 / 1.158 = £21,019  
- **PV total: £66,231**

The present value of the £20,000 residual in 2030 (≈ 4 years): £20,000 / 1.216 = £16,447.

Net present-value comparison:

| Course | Equipment | Operations (PV) | **Total** |
|---|---|---|---|
| Ormscleuch | +£96,000 | — | **£96,000** |
| Trevannock | +£16,447 | +£66,231 | **£82,678** |

On a time-value-adjusted basis Ormscleuch leads by roughly **£13,300**. Without any discounting the lead is still £2,980. Either way the direction is the same.

---

**Where Trevannock could recover ground**

*Spray losses.* The 9 % figure comes from Whinnerdale Bees on the same programme. It is real intelligence, not guesswork, and it works against Trevannock. If losses ran to 15 % — 60 colonies, costing £12,600 — the annual operating surplus drops to £17,740 and the three-season total falls to £53,220, widening Ormscleuch's advantage to nearly £23,000 in nominal terms. There is no plausible scenario in which the spray risk closes the gap rather than widening it.

*Coldharbour and Nyefield.* Two vale growers are asking for a rate for 2028. That is real optionality. If either signed even a modest contract alongside Vantwyn, Trevannock's economics could tip. But neither has committed, no figures exist, and the lorry loses its low-emission-zone permit on 2030-01-01 in any case. Optionality on a depreciating, permit-expiring asset reaching the end of the window is not a strong card.

*The queen-rearing shed.* Ravensgate buys the pallets and the lorry; the shed is not part of either sale. Under both courses the shed stays, so it does not affect the comparison.

---

**Structural picture**

The migratory arm was built on three contracts, all of which lapsed. Vantwyn is a single grower who will not adjust a spray programme that demonstrably kills colonies. After 2029, the lorry is worth a fifth of today's value regardless of what has been earned in the intervening years. The three seasons do not regenerate the business to the position it was in before the contracts lapsed; they merely produce one more cycle on a dwindling asset. Ormscleuch takes the £96,000 at full value, removes spray risk entirely, and leaves 640 colonies earning the heather-and-borage return that has been reliably delivering £143,000 a year with no haulage.

The margin is narrow on raw numbers but widens once time value and spray-loss skew are applied. Simplicity and certainty sit on the same side.

---

READING
Vantwyn's three seasons generate a net operating surplus of £24,340 a season (£67,200 income less £28,400 borage opportunity cost, £7,560 spray replacements and £6,900 haulage). Cumulated over three seasons that is £73,020. The equipment premium sacrificed by not selling to Ravensgate today is £76,000 nominal (£96,000 now versus ~£20,000 residual in 2030). On present-value terms the Ravensgate premium is worth roughly £80,000 and the operating surplus roughly £66,000, so Ormscleuch leads by around £13,000–£14,000. Spray losses can only widen that gap; the Coldharbour/Nyefield optionality is unquantified and the lorry loses its permit before it could be fully exploited. The numbers are close but they consistently point one way.

CALL
ORMSCLEUCH

GROUNDS
The present value of the Ravensgate equipment premium (£96,000 now against a £20,000 rump in 2030) exceeds the discounted net operating surplus from all three Vantwyn seasons, and every realistic move in the spray-loss rate widens that gap rather than closing it.
